ukmt-jmc-2011-01.title: Multiply first
ukmt-jmc-2011-01.body:
Multiplications come before addition: $2\times0\times1=0$, so the value is $0+1=1$.

**Answer: (B) 1**

ukmt-jmc-2011-02.title: Digit sums
ukmt-jmc-2011-02.body:
A number is a multiple of 3 exactly when its digit sum is. The digit sums are $6,9,12,15,18$, all multiples of 3. So all 5 are.

**Answer: (E) 5**

ukmt-jmc-2011-02.title: Three consecutive digits
ukmt-jmc-2011-02.body:
Each number has digits $n-1,n,n+1$, whose sum is $3n$, a multiple of 3. So all five are multiples of 3.

**Answer: (E) 5**

ukmt-jmc-2011-03.title: Count the new cells
ukmt-jmc-2011-03.body:
The normal 'o' has 14 lit cells: a row of 3 at the top and at the bottom, and a column of 4 on each side. In the bold 'o' we light the empty cell to the right of every lit cell. The top row and the bottom row each gain 1 cell (to the right of their last cell), and each of the two side columns gains 4 cells to its right. That is $1+1+4+4=10$ new cells, so $14+10=24$ cells are lit.

**Answer: (B) 24**

ukmt-jmc-2011-04.title: Coins per kilogram
ukmt-jmc-2011-04.body:
1 kg is 100 coins of 10 g. So 100 kg is $100\times100=10\,000$ coins, i.e. £10 000.

**Answer: (C) £10 000**

ukmt-jmc-2011-05.title: Fractions
ukmt-jmc-2011-05.body:
The children received $1-\frac13=\frac23$ of the bar, which is $\frac23=\frac{8}{12}$. At $\frac1{12}$ each, there are 8 children.

**Answer: (B) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2011-05.title: Twelfths
ukmt-jmc-2011-05.body:
$\frac13=\frac{4}{12}$ was left, so $12-4=8$ twelfths were given out, one to each child: 8 children.

**Answer: (B) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2011-06.title: Two triangles
ukmt-jmc-2011-06.body:
The six marked angles are the angles of two triangles. Each triangle's angles sum to $180^\circ$, so the total is $2\times180^\circ=360^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $360^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2011-07.title: Convert to pecks
ukmt-jmc-2011-07.body:
1 barrel $=9$ bushels $=9\times4=36$ pecks. He has picked 1, so he needs $36-1=35$ more.

**Answer: (D) 35**

ukmt-jmc-2011-08.title: Use side lengths
ukmt-jmc-2011-08.body:
Let the square have side $3x$. Its perimeter is $12x$. Each rectangle is $3x\times x$. Going round the octagon the sides are $4x,\,x,\,3x,\,x,\,4x,\,x,\,3x,\,x$ in total $20x$. The ratio is $12x:20x=3:5$.

**Answer: (A) $3:5$**

ukmt-jmc-2011-08.title: Compare perimeters
ukmt-jmc-2011-08.body:
With side $3x$, the square has perimeter $12x$. The octagon fits in a $4x$ by $3x$ rectangle (perimeter $14x$), and the gap cut in the left side adds $2\times3x=6x$ to the boundary. So the perimeter is $14x+6x=20x$. Ratio $12:20=3:5$.

**Answer: (A) $3:5$**

ukmt-jmc-2011-09.title: Divisibility by 9
ukmt-jmc-2011-09.body:
Both numbers have digit sum $45$, so both are multiples of 9, hence their difference is a multiple of 9 and at least 9. It can be 9: $987\,654\,321-987\,654\,312=9$.

**Answer: (A) 9**

ukmt-jmc-2011-10.title: Odd vertices
ukmt-jmc-2011-10.body:
In such a drawing every vertex where the pen passes through uses edges in pairs, so a vertex with an odd number of edges must be the start or the end. The degrees are $P:4$, $Q:2$, $R:3$, $S:3$, $T:2$, so $R$ and $S$ are the only odd vertices and must be the endpoints. Starting at $R$ works: $R\to P\to S\to R\to Q\to P\to T\to S$, and reversing it starts at $S$.

**Answer: (C) only at $S$ and $R$**

ukmt-jmc-2011-11.title: Pentagon angle sum
ukmt-jmc-2011-11.body:
The marked angles $x$ and $y$ (in degrees) are two angles of a pentagon with angles $90,90,300$ (at the triangle's vertex, $360-60$), $x$ and $y$. The angle sum of a pentagon is $540$, so $x+y=540-480=60$.

**Answer: (C) 60**

ukmt-jmc-2011-11.title: Parallel line
ukmt-jmc-2011-11.body:
Draw through the triangle's lower-right vertex a line parallel to the rectangle's long sides. By alternate angles, $x$ and $y$ together make up the triangle's angle of $60^\circ$. So $x+y=60$.

**Answer: (C) 60**

ukmt-jmc-2011-13.title: Add and halve
ukmt-jmc-2011-13.body:
$\frac23=\frac69$, so the sum is $\frac{10}{9}$ and the mean is $\frac12\cdot\frac{10}9=\frac59$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac59$**

ukmt-jmc-2011-14.title: Let the shaded area be $x$
ukmt-jmc-2011-14.body:
The three kinds of face have areas $x,4x,4x$ and each appears twice: $2(x+4x+4x)=18x=72$, so $x=4$ and an unshaded visible face has area $4x=16$ cm².

**Answer: (A) 16**

ukmt-jmc-2011-15.title: Add the half-turn images
ukmt-jmc-2011-15.body:
For rotational symmetry of order 2 each shaded square needs its image under a half-turn about the centre shaded. The three shaded squares have three images, none already shaded, so at least 3 more squares are needed. With these three added, the figure has both diagonals as lines of symmetry, so 3 is enough.

**Answer: (A) 3**

ukmt-jmc-2011-16.title: Bound and construct
ukmt-jmc-2011-16.body:
If the winner had 21 votes, the others would share 62 votes; since $3\times20=60<62$, someone else would get at least 21 votes and there is no outright winner. So the winner needs at least 22. Votes $22,21,20,20$ total 83 and 22 wins.

**Answer: (B) 22**

ukmt-jmc-2011-17.title: Convert to minutes
ukmt-jmc-2011-17.body:
$8$ h $11$ min $=491$ min and $11$ h $5$ min $=665$ min. $\frac{491}{665}\approx\frac{490}{665}=\frac{14}{19}\approx\frac{15}{20}=\frac34$. (Check: $\frac35=0.6$ and $\frac9{10}=0.9$ are much further from $0.74$.)

**Answer: (D) $\frac34$**

ukmt-jmc-2011-18.title: Count the days
ukmt-jmc-2011-18.body:
Every 10 days Peri covers 9 m. After 90 days Peri has covered $81$ m (nine cycles); another 9 days travelling covers the last 9 m. Total $99$ days. $99=14\times7+1$, so he arrives 1 day of the week after Monday: Tuesday.

**Answer: (C) Tuesday**

ukmt-jmc-2011-19.title: Check each digit
ukmt-jmc-2011-19.body:
2, 3, 5 are primes; 11 is prime so 1 appears. A number ending in 4 is even and greater than 2, so not prime. So the digits are 1, 2, 3, 5: four of them.

**Answer: (D) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2011-20.title: Cube size
ukmt-jmc-2011-20.body:
The solid has 7 cubes, each of volume $875\div7=125=5^3$ cm³, so edge 5 cm. Each of the 6 outer cubes shows 5 faces, so there are $30$ faces of area $25$ cm². Surface area $=30\times25=750$ cm².

**Answer: (A) 750**

ukmt-jmc-2011-21.title: Total moving time
ukmt-jmc-2011-21.body:
The moving distance is $27+29=56$ km at 96 km/h, which takes $\frac{56}{96}=\frac7{12}$ h $=35$ minutes. Add the 3 minute stop: 38 minutes, so 09:38.

**Answer: (B) 09:38**

ukmt-jmc-2011-22.title: Equation in pence
ukmt-jmc-2011-22.body:
With $x$ and $y$ stamps: $110x+70y=1000$, i.e. $11x+7y=100$. Then $100-11x$ must be a non-negative multiple of 7. Trying $x=0,\dots,9$ gives $100,89,78,67,56,\dots$; only $x=4$ gives $56=7\times8$. So $y=8$ and the total is $12$.

**Answer: (D) 12**

ukmt-jmc-2011-22.title: Check by mod 7
ukmt-jmc-2011-22.body:
$11x\equiv100\pmod7$ gives $4x\equiv2$, so $x\equiv4\pmod7$. Then $x=4$ ($x=11$ is too many), $y=8$, total 12.

**Answer: (D) 12**

ukmt-jmc-2011-23.title: Isosceles triangles
ukmt-jmc-2011-23.body:
Let $\angle RST=x^\circ$ and $\angle QSU=y^\circ$. Since $x+y+40=180$, $x+y=140$. Triangle $RST$ is isosceles so $\angle R=180-2x$; likewise $\angle Q=180-2y$. So $\angle P=180-(180-2x)-(180-2y)=2(x+y)-180=280-180=100^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $100^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2011-24.title: Shuttle one adult at a time
ukmt-jmc-2011-24.body:
An adult can only cross if a child is waiting on the far side to bring the raft back. Two children cross (1), one returns (2), an adult crosses (3), the other child returns (4): 4 crossings per adult and the situation is as before. Repeat for the second adult (4 more), then the two children cross (1): $4+4+1=9$. No fewer is possible since each adult needs 4 crossings.

**Answer: (D) 9**

ukmt-jmc-2011-25.title: Bounds and examples
ukmt-jmc-2011-25.body:
The three trapeziums have $12$ edges in total; each of the 2 joins removes at least 2 edges, so $N\le8$. A polygon has at least 3 sides, so $N\in\{3,\dots,8\}$. Each of $3,4,5,6,7,8$ can be built (see the official diagrams), so there are 6 values.

**Answer: (C) 6**
